The metabolic physiology of the Cape spiny mouse (Acomys subspinosus) has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions, revealing a maximum basal metabolic rate of 83.46 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 83.46 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This value, obtained through standard indirect calorimetry on post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase, aligns with the moderate metabolic demands expected for a small-bodied murid rodent. Neonates of this species emerge altricial and weigh approximately 2.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.8 grams] at birth, a mass that represents a relatively small maternal investment compared to some other African murids. The rapid postpartum growth trajectory is facilitated by intensive maternal care, including frequent suckling bouts during the initial days of life. Comparative data from related congeners suggest that this neonatal mass is coupled with a protracted period of dependency, allowing for substantial organ development before weaning.

Reproductive output in Acomys subspinosus has been quantified in captive breeding colonies maintained at a controlled temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Under these conditions, females typically produce 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 pups per litter], and available records indicate they can achieve up to 3.5 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 3.5 litters per year], yielding an annual reproductive potential of approximately 10.5 pups per year [Ri = approximately 10.5 pups per year] for a rodent of this size. The ultimate wet weight for adult females has been recorded as 26 grams [Wwi = 26 grams], although body mass can fluctuate between 13 and 26 grams depending on reproductive status, food availability, and seasonal conditions. This upper mass limit is attained after the completion of skeletal growth and reflects the energetic reserves necessary to sustain repeated reproductive events. The species exhibits a clear sexual dimorphism in body size, with males typically remaining smaller than their female counterparts.

Developmental milestones in the Cape spiny mouse have been documented in detail from birth onward. Under standard housing conditions at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], weaning, defined as the cessation of milk ingestion and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs approximately 27 days since birth [tx = approximately 27 days since birth], and sexual maturation, or puberty, is reached considerably later, with individuals attaining reproductive competency at 91 days since birth [tp = 91 days since birth]. The relatively delayed onset of puberty, compared to some other small rodents, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes continued somatic growth and the accumulation of body reserves before the initiation of energy-demanding reproductive activities.

The gestation period of the Cape spiny mouse has been precisely measured in controlled captive populations. Embryonic development proceeds over 27 days [tg = 27 days] when the female is maintained at an ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C]. This gestation length is typical for a murid rodent of this body size and allows for the completion of key organogenic processes before parturition. Following birth, the altricial pups undergo a period of intense growth, first achieving a stable thermal independence as their fur develops and thermoregulatory abilities improve. The interplay between gestation duration and the subsequent lactation period is critical for ensuring that offspring are sufficiently developed to cope with environmental challenges upon weaning.

Longevity records for Acomys subspinosus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3.8 years [am = approximately 3.8 years] under captive conditions held at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], though wild populations likely experience reduced survival due to predation and resource limitation. This value places the species among the longer-lived small rodents, with the combination of a moderate metabolic rate, a relatively long gestation and lactation period, a slow onset of puberty, and an extended lifespan reflecting a comparatively slow-paced life-history strategy for its body size. This pattern of delayed reproduction and enhanced longevity may be an adaptation to the unpredictable resource availability characteristic of its native fynbos and scrubland habitats in South Africa.
